items.question_text: You are the team lead of a group of 10 developers. You provided each developer with an individual Google Cloud Project that they can use as their personal sandbox to experiment with different Google Cloud solutions. You want to be notified if any of the developers are spending above $500 per month on their sandbox environment. What should you do?
items.solution_text: The requirement is to be notified if *any* individual developer exceeds $500, which necessitates tracking spending at the project level rather than aggregating costs. Option A creates a single budget for all projects, so you would only receive alerts when the total collective spend exceeds the threshold, missing individual overages. Option C correctly implements a separate budget per project with configured alerts, ensuring immediate notification if any single sandbox project surpasses the $500 limit.

choices.text: Create a single budget for all projects and configure budget alerts on this budget.
Create a separate billing account per sandbox project and enable BigQuery billing exports. Create a Data Studio dashboard to plot the spending per billing account.
Create a budget per project and configure budget alerts on all of these budgets.
Create a single billing account for all sandbox projects and enable BigQuery billing exports. Create a Data Studio dashboard to plot the spending per project.

items.question_text: You are deploying a production application on Compute Engine. You want to prevent anyone from accidentally destroying the instance by clicking the wrong button. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Enable delete protection on the instance to set the deletionProtection property, which explicitly blocks deletion requests via the Cloud Console or API.
This feature prevents accidental deletion of critical production resources, requiring an administrator with specific permissions to remove the flag before deletion is allowed.

choices.text: Disable the flag "Delete boot disk when instance is deleted."
Enable delete protection on the instance.
Disable Automatic restart on the instance.
Enable Preemptibility on the instance.

items.question_text:
Your company uses a large number of Google Cloud services centralized in a single project. All teams have specific projects for testing and development. The
DevOps team needs access to all of the production services in order to perform their job. You want to prevent Google Cloud product changes from broadening their permissions in the future. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
The requirement to prevent Google Cloud product changes from broadening permissions mandates the use of a custom role, as predefined roles like Project Editor are automatically updated by Google when new permissions are added.
Granting access at the production project level adheres to the principle of least privilege, ensuring the DevOps team has access only where necessary rather than across the entire organization.

choices.text: Grant all members of the DevOps team the role of Project Editor on the organization level.
Grant all members of the DevOps team the role of Project Editor on the production project.
Create a custom role that combines the required permissions. Grant the DevOps team the custom role on the production project.
Create a custom role that combines the required permissions. Grant the DevOps team the custom role on the organization level.

items.question_text:
You are building an application that processes data files uploaded from thousands of suppliers. Your primary goals for the application are data security and the expiration of aged data. You need to design the application to:
* Restrict access so that suppliers can access only their own data.
* Give suppliers write access to data only for 30 minutes.
* Delete data that is over 45 days old.
You have a very short development cycle, and you need to make sure that the application requires minimal maintenance. Which two strategies should you use?
(Choose two.)
items.solution_text:
Option A is correct because Cloud Storage lifecycle management policies automatically delete objects after a specified age (45 days), satisfying the data expiration requirement with zero maintenance.

Option B is correct because signed URLs provide time-limited, granular access control, allowing suppliers to upload data only within the required 30-minute window without needing complex identity management systems.

choices.text: Build a lifecycle policy to delete Cloud Storage objects after 45 days.
Use signed URLs to allow suppliers limited time access to store their objects.
Set up an SFTP server for your application, and create a separate user for each supplier.
Build a Cloud function that triggers a timer of 45 days to delete objects that have expired.
Develop a script that loops through all Cloud Storage buckets and deletes any buckets that are older than 45 days.

items.question_text: Your company wants to standardize the creation and management of multiple Google Cloud resources using Infrastructure as Code. You want to minimize the amount of repetitive code needed to manage the environment. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Cloud Deployment Manager is Google Cloud's native Infrastructure as Code (IaC) service, designed to standardize resource creation and management through reusable templates.
By defining resources in configuration files (YAML/Python), you minimize repetitive code and ensure consistent, reproducible deployments across environments.
Other options like using the Console, curl commands, or bash scripts do not provide a unified IaC framework for managing complex dependencies or reducing boilerplate code effectively.

choices.text: Develop templates for the environment using Cloud Deployment Manager.
Use curl in a terminal to send a REST request to the relevant Google API for each individual resource.
Use the Cloud Console interface to provision and manage all related resources.
Create a bash script that contains all requirement steps as gcloud commands.
